FOR YOU

Your care team plans to start you on two antibiotics given through a vein (IV): clindamycin and gentamicin. This combination is the usual first treatment for infection of the womb after childbirth (postpartum endometritis).

You will likely stay on IV antibiotics until you have had no fever for 24 to 48 hours. Your team will not switch you to tablets just because you are getting better on IV treatment.

If the infection does not improve, your team will review your treatment and may change the antibiotics.

Other options your team may consider are ampicillin-sulbactam and cefoxitin. One study found cefoxitin works about as well as the standard combination. Tablet options exist for places where IV treatment is not possible, but the evidence for them is limited.

Claim: The combination of IV clindamycin and gentamicin is the usual first treatment for postpartum endometritis. Ampicillin-sulbactam and cefoxitin are other options. The evidence for tablet or injection-into-muscle options in low-resource settings is limited.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your clinician has reviewed your situation and has a plan about your Invega Sustenna (paliperidone palmitate) injection dose.

Your dose is planned to go up from 117 mg to 156 mg as a regular maintenance dose. Based on the evidence the clinician checked, you do not need to take oral paliperidone (tablets) to overlap with the new dose. The main thing to know is that the full effect of the higher dose builds slowly. Levels in your body rise gradually over several months, so you may not feel the full change right away.

Your clinician plans to check on you after you have been on the new dose long enough before making any more changes. Oral tablets are usually only used in specific situations, such as a missed injection outside the dosing window or a dose that was not fully given. If you have questions or notice any new symptoms, please contact your clinician.

Claim: For a routine maintenance increase from 117 mg to 156 mg, no oral paliperidone overlap is required, according to the evidence tool. The new steady state takes several months to reach.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is changing your vitamin D medicine between doxercalciferol and calcitriol. These two medicines do not have a proven way to convert dose from one to the other, so your dose will not be switched by simply swapping milligram for milligram. Your doctor will base any dose change on your blood tests instead.

Claim: There is no proven dose conversion between doxercalciferol and calcitriol. A rough rule of thumb (about 1 mcg calcitriol to 2 to 2.5 mcg oral doxercalciferol) is sometimes used as a starting point, but it has not been formally tested, so it is not a guarantee.

What this means for you:
- If you switch medicines, you will likely start on the lowest recommended dose of the new medicine.
- Your doctor will adjust your dose using your intact PTH, calcium, and phosphorus levels.
- You will have blood tests at least every 2 weeks for the first 3 months after starting or changing your dose.
- Doxercalciferol may cause high calcium somewhat less often than calcitriol, but studies have not consistently shown this.
- In the studies reviewed, both medicines lowered PTH by a similar amount (about 35% in one trial of 60 children on peritoneal dialysis), and a Cochrane review of children with kidney disease found no clear differences between them in bone, PTH, calcium, phosphorus, or high calcium.

Please do not change your dose on your own. Call your care team if you have questions or notice symptoms.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your ear pain after swimming or other water activity is most likely caused by acute otitis externa, which is an infection or irritation of the outer ear canal. Your clinician will first ask about your activity, when the pain started, and any dizziness, hearing changes, past ear problems, cotton swab use, diabetes, or weakened immunity. They will then look inside your ear and check for warning signs before deciding on treatment.

Claim: Acute otitis externa is the most likely cause of your ear pain after swimming, but other causes such as pressure injury from diving, bony growths in the ear canal, and, rarely, a more serious infection called malignant otitis externa still need to be ruled out depending on your activities and risk factors.

If the infection is simple, you will usually not need blood tests or scans. Treatment is typically antibiotic or antimicrobial ear drops, sometimes with steroid drops, used for about 7 to 10 days. Keep your ear dry, and do not put cotton swabs or other objects in your ear canal.

If your clinician suspects pressure injury, dizziness, or hearing loss, you may have a hearing test and be referred to an ear specialist. If they suspect the more serious infection, you may need a CT scan, a culture of the ear canal, and urgent specialist care.

Tell your clinician right away if you have severe pain that seems out of proportion to what they see, facial weakness, drainage that does not stop, or no improvement with treatment.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your doctor cannot tell from the current research whether daily physical function (measured by the HAQ questionnaire) is better, worse, or the same on biologic medicine alone compared with a placebo (a dummy treatment). So your treatment decisions will rely on your doctor's direct assessment of you, not on this comparison.

What your care team plans to do:
- Record a HAQ score before you start treatment, so later changes can be compared with your own starting point.
- Check your HAQ score at scheduled visits and watch how it changes over time.
- Talk with you about your personal goals and the everyday tasks that are hard for you, because the HAQ score may not capture all of these.
- Discuss with the rheumatology team whether your treatment should change, and write down the reasons.

Claim: There are not enough data to say whether HAQ function is higher, lower, or the same with biologic monotherapy compared with placebo, and there is not enough evidence to grade the question.

[source: pmid:16162882; pmid:12115176; pmid:24972708]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your surgical team may suggest an antibiotic before your breast cancer operation, since you are not having reconstruction at the same time. Studies suggest that taking antibiotics before surgery lowers the chance of an infection at the surgical site, compared with taking no antibiotic or a dummy pill. The evidence for this is moderate in strength. Your team will check which antibiotic, what dose, and when to give it, and will look for allergies or other personal risks before it is ordered.

Claim: Surgical site infection is lower with preoperative prophylactic antibiotics than with no antibiotic or placebo in breast cancer surgery without reconstruction, with moderate-certainty evidence.

[source: pmid:11063500; pmid:23001082; pmid:16989011; pmid:7480237; pmid:9776150; pmid:23052809; pmid:10873356; pmid:19673597; pmid:2403655; pmid:2403697]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Here is a plain-language summary of the doctors' current thinking about your muscle problem. It is not a final diagnosis.

Claim: Steroid-related muscle damage (steroid myopathy) usually looks normal or nearly normal on the nerve and muscle electrical test (EMG). It does not usually show the signs of active muscle damage that appear in immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM). This is one of the main ways doctors try to tell the two apart. The information behind this comes from a single summary, so your care team will check it against the full medical research and your complete test results before using it to guide your treatment.

What your care team may do next:
- Look closely at your EMG, checking for signs of active muscle damage (fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves). They will test several muscles, because a limited test can miss problems.
- Look at the shape, size, and firing pattern of your muscle electrical signals and how the needle responds when it is placed in the muscle.
- Check your blood level of creatine kinase (CK), a marker of muscle damage. In IMNM it is often much higher than normal. In steroid myopathy it is usually normal or low-normal.
- Test your blood for specific autoantibodies (anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR), and possibly take a small muscle sample (biopsy). These tests are important for a firm IMNM diagnosis.
- Possibly order an MRI of your muscles. This may add information, but the evidence we have does not yet show what it would find.

Some things to keep in mind: the EMG pattern alone cannot tell inflammatory muscle disease apart from other muscle conditions, so several tests are needed together. One figure about how often a certain EMG finding appears in inflammatory muscle disease could not be confirmed, so it is not being relied on here.

Please talk with your doctor about any questions you have about these tests and what the results mean for you.

Claim: Steroid myopathy usually looks normal on EMG, while IMNM shows active muscle damage. Several tests are needed before a diagnosis is made.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: This note explains what the research says about breathing support for premature babies and what your baby's care team plans to do next.

Claim: There is not enough evidence to say whether early or preventive CPAP (a breathing machine that gives steady gentle pressure to the airways) changes the chance of later problems with brain development, compared with supportive care alone. The evidence is not strong enough to rate.

What this means for your baby:
- The question of how CPAP affects later development is still unanswered, so your baby's treatment will not change based on this research alone.
- Your baby will keep getting standard breathing support, following the hospital's usual guidelines. Whether CPAP is used will depend on your baby's breathing and medical needs.
- The team will record your baby's gestational age (how many weeks before birth), birth weight, and breathing status so that progress can be tracked over time.
- Your baby will have routine follow-up visits to check growth and development.
- The studies behind this summary are being reviewed for who they included, when CPAP was started, and how outcomes were measured, before their results are applied to your baby.

Please ask your baby's care team if you have questions.

[source: pmid:15321956; pmid:22402568; pmid:24554040; pmid:3102211]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Based on the evidence we have, heart attack rates are probably about the same for people taking NSAIDs and people taking a placebo (dummy pill). We are fairly confident in this, but not completely certain. Future research could change this picture.

What this means for you:

- This finding shows no clear difference in heart attack risk between NSAIDs and placebo. It does not prove that NSAIDs carry no heart risk at all.
- Before you start or keep taking an NSAID, your doctor will look at your personal heart risk factors, such as blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, and family history.
- NSAIDs can help with pain and inflammation, but they can also have other side effects, such as stomach, kidney, and bleeding problems. Your doctor will talk through these with you so you can weigh the benefits and harms for your situation.
- If your heart health or how often you take an NSAID changes, tell your doctor so the decision can be checked again.

Please ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions about your medicines.

[source: pmid:17111043]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: A sore or blister in the genital area may be caused by several things. Herpes is the most common cause, but syphilis, chancroid, and other causes also need to be checked. Some sores need a small tissue sample (biopsy) to rule out cancer. Looking at the sore alone is often not enough to tell what it is, so tests are needed.

What your doctor plans to do:

- Ask you questions about how long the sore has been there, your sexual history, your age, any recent illness, medicines you take, and any other symptoms, such as eye or mouth problems.
- Look at the sore and the glands in your groin. They will check whether it hurts, feels hard, has clear edges, and whether the glands are tender or swollen.
- Test a swab from the sore for herpes.
- Do a blood test for syphilis. A darkfield microscope test may also be done if it is available.
- Offer an HIV test.
- Take a tissue sample (biopsy) if the sore looks unusual, has not healed in more than 2 to 3 weeks, feels hard, is dark, bleeds, or has not improved with treatment.
- If you are younger and have not been sexually active or had a recent viral illness, your doctor may test for other causes, such as EBV or mycoplasma/ureaplasma.
- Chancroid and some other rarer infections are tested for only if your situation makes them more likely.

The plan depends on these test results. Your doctor will decide on any treatment and will go over the options with you, since treatment is not covered in this note.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: Your risk level cannot be confirmed from the information available yet. Your doctor will first check your exact PSA level and prostate size, because the current information only suggests your PSA may be high.

Here is what this means and what may happen next:

- Your doctor wants to measure your exact PSA level and the size of your prostate. Your PSA level may be high, but this has not been confirmed.
- If your PSA is above 20 ng/mL, you may be placed in a higher-risk group. In that case, your doctor may order scans, such as a bone scan and imaging of soft tissue, to check whether the disease has spread.
- Your doctor may suggest a repeat biopsy, using MRI to guide where samples are taken. The first biopsy may have missed a more serious area, and one MRI finding is unclear.
- If the repeat biopsy still shows low-grade disease, a genetic test on the tissue sample (such as Decipher) may help show how aggressive the cancer is likely to be.
- Active surveillance (watching the cancer closely without immediate treatment) may not be suitable if you are in a higher-risk group. Even in a lower-risk group, certain results could make treatment sooner more appropriate.

Your treating doctor will make the final decision with you. Please ask them any questions you have about these steps.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: If you are with someone who has collapsed and is not breathing normally, and you have not been trained in CPR, you should do chest compressions without stopping. You do not need to stop to give rescue breaths.

Claim: For untrained bystanders doing CPR, keeping up continuous chest compressions without pauses for rescue breaths is linked to higher survival to hospital discharge than stopping compressions to give breaths. The certainty of the evidence is high.

What this means for you:
- Push hard and fast in the middle of the chest, and keep going.
- Do not stop compressions to give rescue breaths.
- This advice is for people who have not been trained in CPR. If you have been trained, follow your training.

[source: pmid:10824072; pmid:20818863; pmid:20818864]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is looking at whether adding a vaccine called MVA85A to the BCG vaccine lowers the chance of getting latent tuberculosis, which is TB bacteria sleeping in the body without causing illness. The studies reviewed so far show no difference in that risk between BCG alone and BCG with MVA85A. The evidence for this is moderate in strength.

What this means for you: your care team plans to keep your current BCG-based prevention and screening plan. They will not change it based on this result alone. They also plan to check the studies directly to confirm that each one is about MVA85A and latent TB. They will look again if new trial results come out, and they may change the plan if a clinical guideline or a specialist advises it.

If you have questions about your prevention or screening, please ask your care team.

Claim: Adding MVA85A to BCG probably does not change the risk of latent tuberculosis, based on moderate-certainty evidence. The current BCG-based plan stays in place.

[source: pmid:25726088; pmid:23391465; pmid:29028973]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your doctor's plan for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), which is when the immune system gets stronger on HIV treatment and starts reacting strongly to an infection you already have, is below in plain words.

- Do not stop your HIV medicine (antiretroviral therapy, or ART) because of IRIS. Keep taking it. The only exception is if IRIS is life-threatening. In that case, your doctor may pause it for a short time.
- For mild IRIS, you may keep taking your ART and your infection medicine, and you may be given an anti-inflammatory pain reliever such as ibuprofen.
- For moderate to severe IRIS, steroids (such as prednisone) can help. In a trial in people with TB-related IRIS, prednisone lowered the number of people who needed hospital stays or surgery. Your doctor will decide the dose and how long to take it, which is usually 2 to 4 weeks, then slowly lowered over 6 to 12 weeks.
- If fluid around the lungs or an abscess gets worse, it may need to be drained.
- The underlying infection changes the plan. For TB meningitis or cryptococcal meningitis, your doctor will choose the best time to start ART, usually 2 to 4 weeks after starting treatment for the infection. Once started, ART continues. For CMV eye infection, ART continues, and eye steroids may be used if inflammation affects the eye. For Kaposi sarcoma, steroids are avoided.
- Overall, about 4.5 out of 100 people with IRIS die from it. The risk is higher, about 20.8 out of 100, for IRIS linked to cryptococcal meningitis.

Claim: ART should generally continue during IRIS and should not be stopped except in life-threatening IRIS.

[source: tool:openevidence]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: This note is about carbohydrate supplements and the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), a serious bowel condition that can affect premature babies.

Claim: Based on very low-certainty evidence, there is no difference in NEC risk between carbohydrate supplementation and no supplementation. The evidence is too uncertain to rule out a meaningful effect in either direction.

The findings come from one randomised clinical trial. It is a single, small study, so it should not by itself change how babies are fed. Your care team will look at local NEC prevention guidance and at your baby's gestational age, how well they tolerate feeds, and their individual risk factors before deciding whether a supplement is right.

[source: pmid:25538834]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your care team is checking whether you have ever taken rofecoxib (also called Vioxx), a pain medicine. Please tell your doctor or pharmacist about any past use of it, and whether you are taking it now.

Claim: In people with mild cognitive impairment (mild memory and thinking problems), Alzheimer's disease appears to occur more often with rofecoxib than with a placebo (dummy pill). This is moderate-certainty evidence, based on one randomized, double-blind study.

Your doctor will weigh this study when deciding whether to avoid or stop this medicine. They will also confirm your current medicine status and your recent memory and thinking assessment with you.

[source: pmid:15742005]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your surgical team is discussing two ways to remove the womb and the tissue around it: a nerve-sparing approach and a standard approach. Your care team will talk with you about which one fits your body and your cancer stage, and whether the nerve-sparing approach is right for you.

Claim: Nerve-sparing surgery may help your bladder recover faster than standard surgery, meaning you may be able to pass urine on your own sooner. The evidence for this is low certainty, so we cannot be sure.

What this means for you:
- Ask your surgical team how the nerve-sparing approach would work for your body and your cancer stage, and whether it is a good choice for you.
- Your bladder recovery may be different with each approach. We do not know a set timeline from the current evidence, so please do not expect a specific number of days.
- After your urinary catheter is removed, your team will measure how much urine stays in your bladder after you pass urine. This shows how well your bladder is recovering. If the amount stays high, your team will step up your care.
- Your plan may change if new or stronger studies become available.

[source: pmid:22209773; pmid:25872890]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Here is what we know about video calls and depression, and what it means for your care.

Claim: We do not know yet whether video calls lead to higher, lower, or the same level of depression after 1 year compared with usual care. The evidence we have is very uncertain.
[source: pmid:22086660]

- Your care will not change based on this evidence alone. It does not show that video calls lower depression.
- We will keep checking your mood regularly with a standard symptom questionnaire, at the start and at follow-up visits.
- Please tell us whether you want video contact and whether you can use it easily. If you do use video calls, we will ask you about your mood and how much contact you have with other people over time.
- The study behind this question was a single study of older adults living in nursing homes who joined a video call program for at least 3 months. Your situation may be different, so it may not apply to you directly.
- We will look at this question again if better evidence becomes available.

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Here is what the doctors' review found about a treatment called percutaneous acetic acid injection (PAI), which is a needle treatment that puts acid into a liver tumor. The question was whether PAI helps people live longer compared with having no treatment.

Claim: There is not enough evidence to say whether PAI makes survival higher, lower, or the same compared with no treatment, so this question cannot be answered with confidence.

The studies found so far compared PAI with other treatments, such as ethanol injection, radiofrequency ablation, or surgery. None of them compared PAI with having no treatment, so they cannot answer this question directly.

What happens next:
- The research team will read the full studies to look for survival results and to check whether any group had no treatment.
- Your liver tumor team will talk about which treatment suits your tumor's size and number, your liver health, and how well you are able to get around and do daily activities.
- The question may be looked at again if newer studies or guidelines come out.

Please do not change your treatment based on this note alone. Talk with your doctor about your options.

[source: pmid:9425919; pmid:16009687; pmid:15973099]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Claim: The effect of antidepressants compared with placebo on depression is uncertain, and the certainty of the evidence is low.

Here is what this means for you:

- The research so far does not clearly show whether antidepressants lower depression more than a placebo (a sugar pill with no active medicine).
- Most of the studies were done in people with inflammatory bowel disease, such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. Because of this, the results may not apply directly to you.
- Whether to start an antidepressant is a choice you and your care team make together. We will weigh the possible benefit, which is uncertain, against possible side effects, and we will take your preferences into account.
- If you start an antidepressant, we will measure your mood with a standard questionnaire when you begin and again at follow-up. This shows whether your mood is improving.

[source: pmid:27664274; pmid:21936344; pmid:26600836]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is looking at whether to routinely check the fluid left in your stomach (called gastric residual monitoring). The current research suggests that routine checks probably lead to more days on intravenous feeding (total parenteral nutrition) than not checking at all. However, the quality of this evidence is low, so this is a tentative finding and not a settled one. Your care team will use it as one factor when deciding what is best for you.

Claim: Compared with no monitoring of gastric residuals, routine monitoring probably leads to more total parenteral nutrition days, but the certainty of this evidence is low.

[source: pmid:25238118; pmid:25166623]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your care team is watching for signs that your tacrolimus level may be too high. Those signs can include shaking (tremor), a rise in your creatinine (a kidney blood test), and high potassium. If you notice any of these, tell your team. They may check a blood level of the drug (a trough level, taken just before your next dose). If the level is at or above your target range, they may lower your dose or pause the drug for a short time. Your kidney function, potassium, magnesium, blood sugar, blood pressure, and nerve symptoms will be checked closely.

Other things to report to your team right away: headache, numbness or tingling, trouble sleeping, severe confusion, seizures, fever or signs of infection, diarrhea, or unusual bleeding or bruising.

Claim: Tremor, rising creatinine, and high potassium are the earliest common signs that tacrolimus may be building up. Lowering the dose often helps these effects, but the exact level that calls for a dose change is not settled by the sources used here, so your team will decide based on your blood tests.

Your team will also talk with you about any medicines that may interact with tacrolimus. Those details need a separate review with them.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your shoulder has suddenly started hurting on the right side. Many different things can cause this, and your doctor will first ask you some questions and examine your shoulder. They may then order X-rays. If the X-rays do not show the cause, they may order an MRI or an ultrasound to look at the muscles and tendons around the shoulder.

Some causes are common, such as a torn or irritated rotator cuff (the group of muscles and tendons that hold the shoulder joint in place), calcium deposits in a tendon, inflammation of the bursa (a small fluid-filled sac that cushions the shoulder), problems at the top of the shoulder where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade, problems in the shoulder joint itself, or a pinched nerve in the neck. Other causes are less common but must not be missed. These include infection in the joint, heart problems, a blood clot in the lungs, and pain from the gallbladder or liver. The plan does not yet say which of these is most likely for you, because more information is needed.

Please get medical help urgently if you have any of the following:
- Fever together with a painful, swollen shoulder
- Chest pain or discomfort
- Trouble breathing
- Heart risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol
- Pain or tenderness in the upper right side of your belly, especially if it is not linked to moving your shoulder

Claim: The most likely causes are rotator cuff injury, acute calcific tendinitis, subacromial bursitis or impingement, AC joint pathology, glenohumeral pathology, and cervical radiculopathy. Septic arthritis, cardiac ischemia, pulmonary embolism, and referred biliary pain must not be missed, and the evidence does not establish which is most likely for you without more context.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your tremor (shaking) may be caused by one of your medicines. This is the most common kind of movement problem caused by medicine. Your care team will go through your full medicine list to look for likely causes. They will also check your caffeine and alcohol intake and look for other causes, such as an overactive thyroid or low blood sugar.

If the tremor is from lithium, your team may check the level of lithium in your blood. A coarser shaking, twitching muscles, or unsteady movements can be signs that the level is too high.

Where it is safe, your team may lower your dose or switch you to a medicine that is less likely to cause tremor. For example, lamotrigine may be used in place of lithium or valproate.

If the medicine cannot be stopped, a medicine called propranolol is often used to ease the shaking. Propranolol can sometimes make depression worse, so your team will weigh this risk with you.

Tremor often gets better after the medicine causing it is stopped or lowered. It may take weeks to months to fully settle.

Claim: Drug-induced tremor usually resolves after the offending drug is stopped or reduced, and a medication review is the recommended first step.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU: Your care team is considering exercise as an extra option, alongside your usual care, to help with flexibility. The evidence that exercise improves flexibility is very weak, so we don't yet know whether it will help you.

Claim: Exercise may improve flexibility compared with usual care, but the evidence for this is very weak, so the benefit is uncertain.

What this means for you:
- Exercise would be added to your usual treatment. It would not replace it.
- We will measure your flexibility at the start and again later, so we can see whether exercise is helping you.
- The study this idea comes from is a single study. Its main focus was fatigue and quality of life in men having radiotherapy for prostate cancer, not flexibility. We are checking it carefully before relying on it.

Please ask your care team any questions you have about exercise before you start.

[source: pmid:17964881]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Here is a short note about computerised cognitive training (CCT), a type of brain-training programme you use on a computer.

Claim: Computerised cognitive training of at least 12 weeks probably leads to higher global cognitive function at the end of intervention than active control interventions, but the certainty of the evidence is low.

What this means for you:
- Computerised cognitive training may help support your overall thinking skills. The studies so far suggest a possible benefit compared with other active activities, but this is not yet certain. Treat it as a tentative finding, not a firm result.
- If you are interested, a course of at least 12 weeks is what the studies looked at.
- Gains may be modest. At the end of the programme, your clinician can check your overall thinking skills to see whether you have benefited.
- Please keep your current cognitive and health supports in place. Training is meant to add to them, not replace them.

Talk with your clinician about whether this option suits you.

[source: pmid:21311196; pmid:29261218]

[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is looking at an infection of the sternoclavicular joint, which is the joint where your collarbone meets your breastbone. This kind of infection is treated like a joint infection, and treatment usually lasts about 4 to 6 weeks of antibiotics. Many people may need the longer end of that range, around 6 weeks, especially if the bone next to the joint is also infected. There is not a single standard plan for this joint, so the length of treatment is set for you individually.

Your doctors will decide how long you need antibiotics based on:
- Whether scans show infection in the collarbone bone or a pocket of pus (an abscess).
- Which germ is causing the infection and which antibiotics it responds to.
- Whether the infection needs to drain.
- How you feel and what your blood tests show over time.

If you are stable, you may be able to switch from antibiotics through a vein to antibiotics by mouth after about 2 weeks. This depends on how well you are improving and on your blood tests. Your team will keep checking your progress and may change your stop date based on how you respond.

Whether you need a procedure to drain the joint is a separate question that is not covered in this note. Please ask your team about it.

Claim: Sternoclavicular joint infection usually needs about 4 to 6 weeks of antibiotics, and about 6 weeks may be needed when bone infection is present. There is not a standard protocol for this joint, so your length of treatment will be individualized.

[source: tool:openevidence]
[AI-generated]

FOR YOU

Your care team is looking into why your gums have grown larger. Here is the plan in plain words.

Claim: The first steps are usually a review of your medicines, a check of your mouth care and past illnesses in your family, and then blood tests and possibly a small tissue sample (biopsy) if the cause is still unclear or a more serious cause is a concern. We do not yet know how well each step predicts the cause, so this order is a general approach and not a confirmed plan.

What your team will do:
1. **Ask questions:** about the medicines you take (some, such as certain blood pressure medicines, seizure medicines, medicines that suppress the immune system, some antibiotics, and birth control pills, can make gums grow). They will also ask about your mouth care, family history of gum problems, pregnancy or puberty, and any symptoms such as tiredness, fever, weight loss, night sweats, bleeding, or easy bruising.
2. **Look at your mouth:** they will note whether the growth is in one area or several, how severe it is, and whether the gums feel firm or soft and bleed easily. They will also check your lymph nodes, spleen and liver, and look for small red or purple spots on your skin.
3. **Blood tests (if a whole-body cause is suspected):** a complete blood count (CBC) with a blood smear. A normal result does not rule out a blood condition, so the test may be repeated if concern remains. Other tests may be added as needed. A bone marrow test is used only if a blood cancer is suspected. A genetic referral may be made if an inherited condition is possible.
4. **Tissue sample (biopsy):** considered if the cause is still unclear after the steps above, or if cancer or leukemia needs to be ruled out. In one study, about 7.5% of localized gum growths were cancerous.
5. **X-rays:** to check the bone around your teeth. A 3D scan may be used in complex cases.

Key point: Swollen gums can sometimes be an early sign of a blood condition called leukemia, even before blood counts look abnormal. Because of this, your team will not rule out a blood cause based on one normal blood test alone.

Please do not stop or change any medicine without talking to your care team first.
